name: Nuppeppō
description: A blob-like Japanese yokai resembling a soft, wrinkled mass of flesh, said to wander abandoned temples and graveyards. Depicted in classic Edo-period yokai scrolls including Toriyama Sekien's Gazu Hyakki Yagyō (1776).
full_description: The Nuppeppō (ぬっぺっぽう) is a yokai of Japanese folklore depicted as an amorphous, wrinkled blob of flesh — roughly humanoid in scale but lacking distinct features beyond rudimentary fingers, toes, and a face suggested by folds of skin. Tradition assigns it no eyes or ears, and it is generally treated as harmless, wandering deserted places: abandoned temples, graveyards, and empty village streets, especially at night and at year's end. Its name derives from nupperi (ぬっぺり), a derogatory term for women wearing heavy makeup, referencing the saggy face. The Nuppeppō is depicted in major Edo-period yokai scrolls including the Bakemono no e (c. 1700, held at Brigham Young University's L. Tom Perry Special Collections), Sawaki Suushi's Hyakkai Zukan (1737), and Toriyama Sekien's Gazu Hyakki Yagyō (1776). A related tradition — the nikujin ('meat-person') reported at Sunpu Castle in 1609 — is sometimes associated with the Nuppeppō; in some lore, eating its flesh confers immortality, echoing Chinese 'feng' or panacea-creature traditions.

origin: Japan; an Edo-period yokai documented in classical Japanese yokai scrolls.

etymology.origin: Japanese, from nupperi (ぬっぺり), a term referring to drooping or sagging — originally a derogatory description of women in heavy makeup
etymology.first_use: Edo period; depicted by name in 18th-century yokai scrolls

timeline.event: A nikujin ('meat-person') is reported at Sunpu Castle (Tokugawa Ieyasu's residence); later commentators connect this incident to Chinese 'feng' panacea-creature lore and to Nuppeppō tradition
Bakemono no e scroll (c. 1700) depicts the Nuppeppō; held at Brigham Young University's L. Tom Perry Special Collections
timeline.significance: Earliest visual attestation of the Nuppeppō by name
timeline.source: Bakemono no e (BYU L. Tom Perry Special Collections)

timeline.event: Sawaki Suushi includes the Nuppeppō in the Hyakkai Zukan (1737)
Toriyama Sekien depicts the Nuppeppō in the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō (1776)
timeline.significance: Most influential and widely-reproduced visual depiction
